slug: 2025-09-10-cn2d7912-土味美学不是设计出来的-而是贫穷生活里自然长出来的
title: Lowbrow aesthetics aren't designed—they naturally emerge from poverty
dek: He explains lowbrow aesthetics not as a style strategy but as something naturally weathered into being by poverty—the way ancient Greek temple columns fade and become beautiful over centuries.
why: Nearly five hours of meandering conversation contains genuine details of his journey from a poor small town to unexpected stardom. Information density is uneven, but the latter half rewards patient listening.
who: Entrepreneurs and content creators interested in indie music ecosystems, grassroots aesthetics, and unexpected viral fame—plus longtime Wu Tiao Ren (五条人) fans.
skip: The opening hour discusses handsomeness and first-love details with low information density—skip ahead to the sections about selling records and forming the band.

points.h: Poverty in his childhood taught him to welcome loss
points.body: Ren Ke (仁科) recalls being a "rich local kid" until elementary school, when his father's businesses—a karaoke bar, hair salon, and tea restaurant—failed in sequence. His own grilled meat stall folded within two months after he kept giving free food to friends. This boom-and-bust pattern shaped his later "unambitious" creative mindset: he never expected music to earn money or make him a rock star, just enjoyed making it.

points.h: Picture someone always too late to be born, and panic fades
points.body: Around age 17, Ren Ke conceived of a fictional person named Mr. X (X先生)—someone who always missed every era, forever waiting to be born, never arriving even before the universe ended. He applies this thought experiment to himself: perhaps he's the person who "never gets an album out," but that's not failure, just not his turn yet. This coherent worldview let him spend years selling books and singing in Guangzhou with zero commercial expectations while maintaining emotional stability.

points.h: No sales training, but he made over 100 yuan a day
points.body: After arriving in Guangzhou to meet A Mao (阿茂), Ren Ke made money selling pirated books—clearing over 100 yuan on day one, faster than A Mao's bootleg CD business. He refused A Mao's pirated records and tried selling ties but found it "more shameful than selling pirated books." He describes himself as "overconfident" and "lucky," even reserving stall space for philosophy by Freud and Nietzsche that barely sold, reasoning that "someone eventually buys everything."

points.h: They pushed the unplugged format to its logical extreme
points.body: During their record shop era, they invited Zhou Yunpeng (周云蓬)—who was accepting an award—to play an "unplugged" set. Zhou expected typical unplugged: speakers but no effects. Instead he arrived to find they literally had no PA system, only speakers for playback—genuine a cappella plus acoustic guitar. Zhou nearly fell apart but still performed and sold albums. This poverty characterized their early tours: sound equipment stolen by audience members to charge phones, PA and monitor mixed on one channel, lights never changing once all night.

points.h: Aesthetics don't get installed—they're naturally worn into being
points.body: Luo Yongzao (罗永浩) proposes a theory: humans don't initially see peeling paint and cracks as beautiful—that was stuff needing immediate repair. But after decades of weathering accumulate, people suddenly notice rough surfaces have intrinsic beauty. Ancient Greek temple columns started painted but only became the gray-white we know today after centuries of finish loss. Ren Ke agrees and adds that plastic buckets and salon signs have "touch" with his real experience—authentic lived texture, not a style strategy grafted afterward.

points.h: One forgotten poster becomes their most iconic visual symbol
points.body: Wu Tiao Ren (五条人) wanted a striking logo like Rolling Stone's tongue. Designer Hu Zi (胡子) drew over 30 options but nothing clicked. The solution came from a poster Hu Zi had painted for a previous tour—a plastic bag caught in wind like a sunset above workers, captioned with "Tomorrow's sun will rise for you." Ren saw it and realized: why not just use this as the logo? One plastic bag became the band's most recognizable visual identity.

points.h: One defiant song choice makes the whole country smile
points.body: A Mao (阿茂) initially refused The Summer of Bands entirely. Ren spent two hours on an emotional "guilt trip" call convincing him to perform. By late-night taping, both were exhausted in the wings—even the backing band urged A Mao not to take risks, worried about job security. Ren chose the most "frivolous" track deliberately, thinking they'd bomb fast and be eliminated anyway. Instead that spite-chosen song made the whole country laugh, becoming one of the show's most viral moments.

points.h: Post-fame fans nearly drove him into the ocean
points.body: At an Alaya (阿拉雅) beachside show that sold thousands of tickets, at the post-show party, 40-50 fans chased Ren Ke for autographs and photos, pushing him deeper toward the water until crew extracted him into a car. He says that's when he finally understood why celebrities like Leslie Cheung and Andy Lau complained about crowds—he'd briefly tasted "Four Heavenly Kings" problems himself. Since then he wears plain masks and hats, bought expensive ones then kept losing them, so switched to cheap ones.

terms.def: A fictional character Ren Ke imagined to represent someone who perpetually arrives too late for any era and never gets born
A thought experiment where your future self travels back to the present to reconcile with your past
Bob Dylan's approach of spontaneously disrupting arrangements in live performance and refusing to repeat yourself

quotes.text: There's this person who's had it a bit worse than us. Like you, born right now—you'd miss every era. I was thinking, what if there was such a person? And I decided: this person, Mr. X. Mr. X missed every era, and right until the universe ended, he never got born.
I just sold books—that's all. Made over 100 yuan on my first day. I thought, wow, this money's so easy to make. God, I was dead broke then, 350 yuan a month.
Never expected that once he showed up we wouldn't even have speakers—just the music playback one. Nothing at all. No, I mean—we had zero live performance equipment. That's truly unplugged.

But when this accumulates over time, one day people suddenly realize this broken, worn-down thing has a kind of natural beauty. And that's when the aesthetics emerge. It was never designed to begin with.
I loved Ruling Stone so much—their logo was incredibly striking back then. That tongue.

If I played that other song and flopped, I'd still be eliminated but have to go back and keep making music with this band. But if I chose this one, we'd all go down happy together, and then go back and reflect. Except I never imagined the whole nation would go down happy with us.
I was chased by about 40 to 50 people. Nearly torn to shreds by fans—nearly—then I almost ended up swimming out into deep ocean.
